body_es: GitFlow es un modelo de ramificación que asigna un propósito fijo a cada tipo de rama. `develop` acumula el trabajo integrado que aún no se ha publicado; desde ahí nacen las ramas `feature/*` para construir una funcionalidad concreta, que se fusionan de vuelta a `develop` al terminar. Cuando `develop` está listo para publicarse, se crea una rama `release/*` donde solo se corrigen detalles finales, nunca se añaden funcionalidades nuevas; al cerrarla, se fusiona tanto en `master` como en `develop` y se etiqueta la versión. Las ramas `hotfix/*` parten directamente de `master` para arreglar un problema en producción sin esperar al próximo ciclo de release, y también se fusionan en ambas ramas para que el arreglo no se pierda. Esta estructura da trazabilidad clara sobre qué está en producción y qué está en desarrollo, y funciona bien en equipos grandes con ciclos de release planificados. Un error común es aplicar GitFlow completo a un proyecto pequeño con despliegues frecuentes: el peso de mantener tantas ramas paralelas frena la entrega sin aportar el beneficio que sí tiene en un producto con versiones formales y equipos numerosos.
body_en: GitFlow is a branching model that assigns a fixed purpose to each type of branch. `develop` accumulates integrated work that has not been released yet; from there, `feature/*` branches are created to build a specific piece of functionality, merging back into `develop` when finished. When `develop` is ready to ship, a `release/*` branch is created where only final details are fixed, never new features; when it closes, it merges into both `master` and `develop` and the version gets tagged. `hotfix/*` branches start directly from `master` to fix a production problem without waiting for the next release cycle, and they also merge into both branches so the fix is not lost. This structure gives clear traceability about what is in production and what is in development, and it works well for large teams with planned release cycles. A common mistake is applying full GitFlow to a small project with frequent deployments: the overhead of maintaining so many parallel branches slows delivery down without providing the benefit it does have in a product with formal versions and large teams.
example_code:
class GitFlow:
    def __init__(self):
        self.branches = {"master", "develop"}
        self.log = []

    def start(self, kind, name):
        prefixes = {"feature": "feature/", "release": "release/", "hotfix": "hotfix/"}
        base = "develop" if kind in ("feature", "release") else "master"
        branch = prefixes[kind] + name
        self.branches.add(branch)
        self.log.append(f"iniciado {branch} desde {base}")
        return branch

    def finish(self, kind, name):
        prefixes = {"feature": "feature/", "release": "release/", "hotfix": "hotfix/"}
        branch = prefixes[kind] + name
        target = "develop" if kind == "feature" else "master"
        self.branches.discard(branch)
        self.log.append(f"fusionado {branch} en {target} (y en develop si aplica) y eliminado")
        return target


flow = GitFlow()
branch = flow.start("feature", "authentication")
print(f"rama activa: {branch}")
target = flow.finish("feature", "authentication")
print(f"fusionada en: {target}")

flow.start("release", "1.0.0")
flow.finish("release", "1.0.0")

for line in flow.log:
    print(line)
print("ramas restantes:", sorted(flow.branches))

source: Vincent Driessen — A successful Git branching model — https://nvie.com/posts/a-successful-git-branching-model/
